questions.question: Describe the kingdom of Mapungubwe.
questions.expected_answer: Mapungubwe, in Limpopo where the Limpopo and Shashe rivers meet, was a wealthy African kingdom at its greatest from about 1220 to 1290. Its people farmed sorghum and millet and kept cattle. Society was divided into classes: the sacred king and royal family lived on top of the hill and ordinary people below. It declined after about 1300 when the climate became drier, and power moved to Great Zimbabwe.

questions.question: Describe the golden objects of Mapungubwe and what they tell us.
questions.expected_answer: In 1933, gold objects were found in royal graves on the hill, including the golden rhinoceros, made of thin gold sheets over a wooden core fixed with tiny gold nails, a golden bowl, a sceptre and thousands of gold beads. They show that craftspeople were skilled goldsmiths, that gold was a sign of royal status, and the rhino may have symbolised the king's power.

questions.question: Why is Mapungubwe important heritage?
questions.expected_answer: It shows that a wealthy, organised African kingdom existed in southern Africa long before Europeans arrived, with skilled craftspeople and trade across the Indian Ocean to Arabia, India and China, bringing glass beads, cloth and celadon. It is a World Heritage Site and national park, the golden rhino is a national symbol on the Order of Mapungubwe, and the reburial in 2007 showed respect for ancestors.
